1.pericope_label: The year of release; the creditor’s hand; the foreigner excepted

schools.summary: Set out both readings of the release and prefer permanent cancellation, hedged by conditions — an Israelite debtor, poor, who borrowed for subsistence — while holding a solvent debtor bound in conscience though not in law.

Deny that the release touched servants and fix it at the opening of the seventh year rather than its close; justify the exception of foreigners by their being outside the covenant; and read the whole statute as a restraint on accumulated wealth, framed to preserve a condition of mediocrity and so the nation’s liberty.
Place the law as an extension of the earlier sabbatical legislation, and distinguish the alien of another nation from the resident foreigner in order to show that the exception implies no hostility.
Follow the same account of the release and identify the year with the sabbatical year, referring the reader back to the earlier statutes rather than expounding them again.

debates: Whether the release extinguished the debt permanently or merely stayed the suit for that year — Henry reports both and prefers the first.
When in the seventh year the release took effect: at its beginning (Gill, arguing that otherwise it would be no year of rest) or simply during it.
Whether the release applied to servants as well as debts — denied by Gill, who distinguishes the sabbatical year from the jubilee.

Why foreigners were excepted: because they suffered no loss of income in the seventh year and a creditor’s ordinary right stands (Keil), or because despisers of the Law had no title to a benefit given to the elect people (Calvin).
outliers: Calvin alone gives an economic and political rationale — that the law existed to prevent a wealthy few from tyrannising over the rest.
Keil alone anticipates and rebuts the charge that the foreigner clause is xenophobic.
Wesley’s comment on this passage is Henry’s, abridged nearly verbatim.

4.pericope_label: No poor among you; the blessing, the lending and the ruling

schools.summary: Take the clause as a real exception exempting the solvent, refuse the reading that makes it a promise, and derive the whole blessing from the covenant — so that poverty in Israel would be evidence of the people’s own depravity, and the promise of produce is conditional on their liberality.

Settle the clause by grammar — a jussive, hence an imperative not to create poverty (Keil), or a purpose clause (Ellicott) — reconcile it with the later admission that the poor never cease, work the vocabulary of pledging and lending, and trace the clause forward to the community of goods in Acts.
Prefer the marginal purpose-clause rendering, so that the verse gives the reason of the law, and dispose of the apparent contradiction by taking the promise comparatively.

debates: What save when there shall be no poor means: an exception where none are poor (Gill), a promise that none will be (reported by Gill from the Targum), a purpose clause giving the law’s reason (Wesley, Ellicott), a jussive command not to make the poor poorer (Keil), or a comparative statement (Clarke).
Whether the clause contradicts the later assurance that the poor will never cease from the land — Keil and Clarke each resolve it differently.
Whether lending to many nations and ruling over them is prediction or rhetorical amplification (Calvin takes the second).
Whether the promised blessing means universal prosperity or only that no one is left in want (Ellicott argues the second).
outliers: Ellicott alone reads the verse as the source of the description of the Jerusalem church in Acts, and alone enlists Rashi in support.
Calvin alone concludes that poverty among the Israelites would prove the people’s own wickedness.

7.pericope_label: The poor brother; the wicked thought; open thine hand wide

schools.summary: Treat the promise of no poor as conditional and defeated by Israel’s disobedience; personify the heart of Belial as Satan’s working; require the heart opened before the hand; and press the timing, that relief be given at the opening of the release year as though repayment were days away.

Reconcile the two statements by distinguishing falling into poverty from remaining in it, and ground its permanence in providential discipline; parse the wicked thought grammatically; and import Rashi’s practical rulings wholesale as the best commentary on the law.

Read the belial heart as simply good-for-nothing, expound the evil eye against the single eye as covetousness against liberality, treat the perpetuity of the poor as God’s provision for exercising compassion, and allow no measure of charity but the other’s need and one’s own ability.

debates: How the promise of no poor stands with the poor never ceasing: a forfeited condition (Gill), a distinction between falling into want and remaining in it (Ellicott), a providential ordinance for discipline (Keil), a mercy that keeps compassion in exercise (Clarke), or no contradiction at all since the earlier verse only forbade abandoning the destitute (Calvin).
Whether the wicked heart is a heart of Belial in the personal sense (Gill) or belial as an adjective meaning worthless (Clarke, Keil).
Whether the poor may be given more than bare necessity — Rashi’s rulings, reported by Ellicott, allow a horse to ride on while denying any duty to make him rich.
outliers: Ellicott alone declares his method, that he is transcribing Rashi almost entire in order to show the Jews understood Christian charity from Moses.
Clarke alone says that without the poor a man would become a Stoic or a brute.
Ellicott alone states that God will never make all men absolutely equal in this world.
Calvin alone times the relief to the opening of the release year.

12.pericope_label: The Hebrew servant released in the seventh year and furnished liberally

schools.summary: Take the seventh year as the seventh of service and not the sabbatical year (Keil) — or the reverse (Ellicott) — trace the Egypt motive through the whole law, and read the provision for released thieves as a standing rebuke to modern practice.

Press the Hebrew for a loading that is honourable as well as generous, while denying that the law aimed at enriching the freed man or at coercing the unwilling giver; ground the obligation in the brotherhood of Hebrew slaves, who must not fare worse than hirelings.
List the three ways a Hebrew came into servitude, note the jubilee as an additional discharge, and draw the principle that God’s people are a free people not to be held in perpetual slavery.

Compute the six years from the start of service, itemise what the flock, floor and winepress were to yield and why the freed man needed them, and read the spoils of Egypt as withheld wages that God paid.

debates: Whether the seventh year is the seventh of the man’s service (Keil, Wesley, Henry) or the sabbatical year whenever it fell (Ellicott) — on Ellicott’s view a slave would rarely serve six full years.
How liberal the furnishing was meant to be: as much as the man can carry, and honourably (Gill), or enough for a fresh start but expressly not enrichment (Calvin).
Whether the law is enforceable or an appeal to willing generosity — Calvin denies it is a civil enactment for extorting from the avaricious.
Why the law is repeated here when it already stands in Exodus — Keil denies it was to extend it to women.
outliers: Ellicott alone turns the law into a criticism of his own country, judging Christian England to fall short of Mosaic provision for discharged thieves.
Gill alone finds in the verb for furnishing the sense of ornamental chains, and so an honourable discharge.
Wesley alone treats the spoils of Egypt as unpaid wages justly recovered.

16.pericope_label: The servant who will not go out; the awl; a double hired servant

schools.summary: Justify the option of perpetual service as a guard against a manumission that would amount to abandonment; harmonise the maidservant’s release with the apparently contrary earlier statute; and reject both current explanations of the double wages.

Locate the boring of the ear at the court rather than the master’s house, on rabbinic authority; leave the double wages undecided between two readings; and take the verse’s purpose to be the reproof of grudging enfranchisement.
Allow for ever to reach only to the jubilee, and read the clause about the maidservant as covering both liberal dismissal and perpetual service alike.

debates: Whether the ear was bored at the master’s door, as the text seems to say, or at the door of the court (Gill, from the Targum of Jonathan).
Whether for ever means lifelong (Keil) or only until the jubilee (Wesley).
What worth a double hired servant means: that slaves worked harder than paid labourers, or that six years is twice a hireling’s usual term — Calvin offers both, Keil rejects both.
Whether the maidservant’s release contradicts the earlier statute — Ellicott denies it, distinguishing the manner of going out from the fact of it.
outliers: Keil alone defends the option of lifelong service as a mercy, on the ground that freedom without prospects is a kind of expulsion.
Ellicott alone works out the position of an unmarried female slave and concludes her rights matched a man’s.

19.pericope_label: The firstlings sanctified; the blemished firstling eaten in thy gates

schools.summary: Refer the prohibition on working and shearing to the female firstlings specifically, on Patrick’s authority, and ground the whole law in thankful remembrance of the sparing of Israel’s firstborn in Egypt.

Read the prohibition of the firstborn generally and explain it by the temptation to use the animal first and offer it deteriorated afterwards; generalise from the necessity of such a law to the greed of men who will cheat God himself.

Reconcile this precept with the assignment of firstlings to the priests by distinguishing two collections in the year; and resolve the apparent contradiction between sanctifying the firstling and being forbidden to sanctify it, by distinguishing recognition of God’s property from a voluntary vow.

Follow the female-firstling reading and require even these to be offered as peace offerings; and take the eating to belong to the annual feasts, remarking that God makes duty and interest run together.

debates: Whether the ban on working and shearing concerns the female firstlings only (Henry, Wesley, and bishop Patrick) or the firstborn generally (Keil, Calvin).

Who eats the firstling, given that the firstlings are elsewhere assigned to the priests: the priest is addressed here (Rashi, reported by Ellicott and by Gill under his other name); the unblemished go to the priest and the unfit to the owner; or two separate collections in the year account for both (Ellicott’s own preference).
How thou shalt sanctify stands with the rule that no man shall sanctify a firstling — resolved by Ellicott alone.
outliers: Calvin alone argues from the existence of the law to the depravity of the men it was written for.
Clarke alone answers Satan’s question about Job from this verse, and answers it in the affirmative.
